@edhgoose This doesn't make sense to me, for two reasons:
- It only happens to work in your particular scenario because for your repo the time for `git status --untracked-files=all` happens to be above the retry threshold, but `git status --untracked-files=normal` happens to be below it. That is not necessarily true for other repos; I made an extremely huge one for testing, where `=all` takes ~15s and `=normal` takes ~10s, so in that repo your fix doesn't help.
- The user experience is unacceptable. If you create a new directory with a new file in it, how would you stage that? It would require some new feature where you can override the `=normal` on demand so that you see the new file (a bit like typing `git add newdir/newfile` manually). I don't want to invest in adding such functionality. Or it would have to be opt-in for users who know they will never need to add new files to their repo; but that opt-in already exists, it's the git config.

What we should do next is find out if it is lazygit itself that causes the error for you guys, or some other app running in the background.
1. Lazygit itself: with the huge test repo mentioned above I can easily reproduce the error by not waiting long enough. When I focus the lazygit terminal window it makes a refresh involving a `git status` call, and if I don't wait those 10s (or 15s depending on the config), the next lazygit command like staging a file shows the error. The same happens when performing a lazygit command (e.g. press space to stage a file) and then not waiting long enough before performing the next one. Please try (both of you) if you can still reproduce the error when waiting long enough after bringing lazygit to the front, and between actions.
2. Other programs: I'm just guessing here, but I can imagine git clients that use a file watcher to get notified of when they need to refresh their UI (Sublime Merge is an example of that), and then make `git status` calls without `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0`. If they manage to start that call before lazygit makes its own post-command refresh, and that status takes longer than lazygit's ~1.2s retry interval, then this would totally explain the error. So if you are running git clients that you suspect could play a role here (e.g. fugitive or Goland), try quitting them and see if you can still reproduce the error.

As for possible solutions: of course 1. is unacceptable, users shouldn't have to wait between commands to avoid errors. A simple improvement could be to simply increase the retry interval; bailing out on an index.lock that is genuinely stale (e.g. after a git process crashed) is a one-time thing where users have to delete the file, and I'd say it doesn't matter too much if that error appears after 1s or 5s. A more thorough solution could be for lazygit to track its own foreground status calls (after a focus-in or after a command), and wait for them instead of handling these through the normal retry loop heuristic. That requires a little more code, but may well be worth it.

For 2.: if we do indeed find one that is responsible, the only thing to do there is to report an issue to them to suggest adding `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` (or `--no-optional-locks`) to their background status calls. Nothing we can do on our side to fix that, except for increasing the retry threshold.

Confirmed on Windows with Git 2.55.0.windows.3 using a freshly initialized reftable repository.

After the first empty commit:
- .git/HEAD still contains ref: refs/heads/.invalid
- git branch --show-current returns master
- git symbolic-ref --short HEAD also returns master

The current getCurrentBranch implementation reads .git/HEAD directly, so the .invalid label is deterministic for this repository format even though Git resolves the branch correctly. This reproduces the report on a second OS and suggests that querying Git, instead of interpreting HEAD on disk, is the format-independent boundary.

Interestingly, trying to create a reproducer also led me to a workaround!

```sh
# Copy the migrated config to a temp dir
TEMPDIR=$(mktemp -d)
cd ~/.config/lazygit/ && cp $(readlink ~/.config/lazygit/config.yml) $TEMPDIR

# Start lazygit with the migrated config from the temp dir
cd $DOTFILES
lazygit -ucf $TEMPDIR/config.yml 
```

Yes, it's true that lazygit is invoked as a child process again during the rebase, and that it tries to migrate the config again there. I think it should be easy to avoid this; the child instance doesn't need the config for anything as far as I can see, so it should simply not load it at all. I can look into this when I find some time.

However, if you stop mid-rebase because of a conflict, and then switch to your editor to resolve conflicts, the moment you return to lazygit it will try to load the config again, and migrate it at that point. That is correct and unavoidable (I think), so you'll have to pay attention to that; the changed config file will appear as an unstaged change in the Files panel, so you can just discard the modification there.

An optional ahead/behind display relative to the base branch could help with this use case.

For a hypothetical example, suppose two feature branches both track their own remote branches and are fully synced with them. Both are 20 commits behind `main`, but one branch's history is already contained in `main`, while the other still has 3 commits that `main` does not contain. With the current behind-only display, both show `✓` and `↓20`, so scanning the branch list does not reveal that difference.

An opt-in display could make it visible:

```text
                         relative to main
feature-a  ✓             ↓20 ↑0
feature-b  ✓             ↓20 ↑3
```

Could `showDivergenceFromBaseBranch` offer a mode that shows both counts, while preserving the existing defaults? This would compare against the detected base branch, which is a slightly different scope from this issue's proposal to compare against the currently checked-out branch.

I found the earlier discussion in [#3536](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/issues/3536#issuecomment-2094065324), where the usefulness of ahead counts was acknowledged but the extra visual noise was a concern. Since [#4785](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/pull/4785) moved the base-divergence indicator to the right, perhaps an optional two-count mode would now fit better while keeping it separate from upstream status.

The counts would describe commit ancestry only. A nonzero ahead count can remain after a squash or rebase merge, so this should not be presented as a definitive PR-merged or safe-to-delete indicator. The benefit is being able to distinguish branches with unique commits from branches whose history is already contained in the base, directly in the list.

<details>
<summary>Possible configuration and implementation pointers</summary>

For example, users could opt in through their LazyGit `config.yml`:

```yaml
gui:
  # Proposed new value; NOT currently supported.
  showDivergenceFromBaseBranch: aheadAndBehind
```

`aheadAndBehind` is only a suggested name. The existing `none`, `onlyArrow`, and `arrowAndNumber` modes would keep their current behavior; users could switch back to `arrowAndNumber` for behind-only numbers.

Looking at the current source, these seem like the relevant places to extend:

- [`pkg/config/user_config.go`](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/blob/d0ede21e9c1e13de255b78f28102450d4523d748/pkg/config/user_config.go#L187): add the new supported value to the config definition/schema and update the generated configuration documentation.
- [`pkg/commands/git_commands/branch_loader.go`](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/blob/d0ede21e9c1e13de255b78f28102450d4523d748/pkg/commands/git_commands/branch_loader.go#L148): retain both counts for the same selected base. The Git >= 2.41 path already parses both via `%(ahead-behind:...)`, but `selectBehindForBranch` returns only behind; the legacy `rev-list --left-right --count` query also returns both. Carry the pair through refreshes instead of discarding ahead.
- [`pkg/commands/models/branch.go`](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/blob/d0ede21e9c1e13de255b78f28102450d4523d748/pkg/commands/models/branch.go#L39): store both base-relative counts, with a way to distinguish a valid result from unknown/not-yet-loaded data. Currently `BehindBaseBranch == 0` also means not yet determined, so it would be misleading to render an explicit `↑0` before a successful calculation.
- [`pkg/gui/presentation/branches.go`](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/blob/d0ede21e9c1e13de255b78f28102450d4523d748/pkg/gui/presentation/branches.go#L253): extend `divergenceStr` to render the pair in the new mode, including ahead-only branches where behind is zero, while retaining the existing right-aligned placement.

The existing branch-loader, branch-presentation, and `show_divergence_from_base_branch` integration tests would be natural places to cover ahead-only, behind-only, diverged, equal, and unknown states, plus unchanged behavior for the existing modes.

These are implementation pointers rather than a tested patch; the exact config name and data representation would be up to the maintainers.

</details>

> An optional ahead/behind display relative to the base branch could help with this use case.

Hi @stefanhaller - thanks for your detailed reply. Sorry for the very slow response - I've not had time to focus on this issue. Regarding your questions: * No, I do not experience the problem if I wait. If I ensure the UI has updated to show my action is completed before attempting another action, then I do not trigger the index lock. If I try and rapid fire add multiple files, then I do experience the issue. * I experience the locking problem without any other git tools (my primary tool is Goland) running. I do have Sublime installed, but not with Sublime Merge. My research shows no other git processes running, except for the `git fsmonitor--daemon`. With your large repo - do you have the setting [feature.manyFiles](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#Documentation/git-config.txt-featuremanyFiles) turned on? I've realised that's automatically turned on for me at my workplace, which in turn activates the [core.untrackedCache](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#Documentation/git-config.txt-coreuntrackedCache). I think the key difference I'm seeing between the `--untracked-files=all` and `--untracked-files=normal` is that `all` can't / doesn't use the untrackedCache, which is why the performance difference is so stark. It's sub second for `normal` and multi-second for `all`. I've turned these settings (`feature.manyFiles` and `core.untrackedCache`) off, as well as the suggested `showUntrackedFiles normal` change recommended from the comment above, and removed the cache index: ``` git config set core.untrackedCache false git config set feature.manyFiles false git config unset status.showUntrackedFiles # Ensuring the cache is removed: git update-index --no-untracked-cache time git status --untracked-files=normal --porcelain -z --find-renames=50% 0.38s user 1.69s system 89% cpu 2.312 total time git status --untracked-files=all --porcelain -z --find-renames=50% 0.39s user 1.62s system 108% cpu 1.856 total ``` You can see the timing is pretty similar. Then turning the untrackedCache back on to confirm the difference is stark again: ``` git config set core.untrackedCache true # Populate the cache: time git status --untracked-files=normal --porcelain -z --find-renames=50% 0.44s user 1.83s system 106% cpu 2.133 total time git status --untracked-files=normal --porcelain -z --find-renames=50% 0.20s user 0.25s system 119% cpu 0.376 total ``` The time taken is significantly lower for `normal`. And now with all: ``` time git status --untracked-files=all --porcelain -z --find-renames=50% 0.38s user 1.71s system 107% cpu 1.938 total # Again to prove it's not just a cache warmup problem: time git status --untracked-files=all --porcelain -z --find-renames=50% 0.39s user 1.67s system 107% cpu 1.916 total ``` Regarding your suggestion for lazygit to wait for its other commands to finish, I think the challenge with that is that the experience for the user could still be very poor if the UI doesn't allow interaction or update between those actions. i.e. at the moment if you undertake several actions (e.g. adding multiple files), the UI hangs while the actions block waiting for the command to retry. I wonder if instead of the feature changes, a better solution would be some documentation on recommended git settings for working with large repos? Which I think is to turn on these settings in _git_: Well documented elsewhere on using large repos: ``` git config feature.manyFiles true ``` Override the default lazygit behaviour for untracked-files all, which has the downside of a poor UX for adding new directories as shown below but should otherwise improve performance: ``` git config status.showUntrackedFiles normal ``` I don't perceive the UX to be too poor - it only affects files added to new directories: This is the default behaviour with `all`: This is the behaviour with `showUntrackedFiles normal`: The files within the new directory don't show (but the file within the existing directory does): And when you add the directory, the files show: There's obviously a downside if you don't wish to add the whole folder - but I don't personally mind. May be up to personal opinion!

What was going on here: in the `--- a/Directory With Space/foo.txt` line, git appends a `\t` whenever the path contains spaces; it's invisible above. This tab is actually significant and is needed for parsing the diff header correctly. What was happening is that gocui renders the diff content into the view, at which time the tab gets expanded to spaces; then, lazygit takes the view's cell content and parses it again as a diff, which fails because the tab got lost.

To fix this, a gocui view now retains the original input alongside the rendered cells, and the diff parser can use that to faithfully reconstruct the original diff. See b0a188236305.

As for "highlighting still looked quite broken": this is intentional, see ee59554c97ea. It looks a little weird when a single line is selected, but it makes more sense when a whole change block is selected, and especially with a diff renderer like delta.

I ran into this as well. It shows up when a branch forks off a merge commit. In the merge's row, the branch's line ends in some column, and the merge's line to its second parent starts in the same column. Both land in one cell and render as a straight `│`. The branch then seems to sit on the merge's second parent:

```
◎─╮      merge feature-a
│ ○      a1              parent: base
◎─│─╮    merge feature-b
│ │ ○    b1              parent: base
◎─│─╯    base (a merge)
│ ○      x1              looks like a1's parent
○─╯
```

I've fixed it on my fork without changing the layout, see draft PR #6060. Without a selection, the lines from a merge's children into the merge take priority and stay connected:

```
◎─│─╮    merge feature-b
│ │ ○    b1
◎─┴─╯    base
│ ○      x1
○─╯
```

The gap leaves open which commit x1 was merged into, but no line points at the wrong commit anymore.

A selected commit's lines are drawn on top, without crossings. The merge's connection to its second parent is only shown when the merge is selected, as with base here. Selecting b1 runs its line to base over a1's, and selecting a1 ends its line with a curve next to b1's:

```
base selected         b1 selected           a1 selected
│ ○     a1            │ ○     a1            │ ○     a1
◎─│─╮                 ◎─│─╮                 ◎─│─╮
│ │ ○   b1            │ │ ○   b1            │ │ ○   b1
◎─╮─╯   base          ◎───╯   base          ◎─╯─╯   base
│ ○     x1            │ ○     x1            │ ○     x1
○─╯                   ○─╯                   ○─╯
```

This also fixes #4246. On master, selecting merge feature-b cuts a1's and b1's lines off from base (`◎ │─╯`). On the branch they stay connected (`◎─┴─╯` if a1 and b1 share an author, `◎─╯─╯` otherwise).

```
main                      branch
○        t0               ○        t0
│ ○      a1   (alice)     │ ○      a1   (alice)
│ │ ○    b1   (bob)       │ │ ○    b1   (bob)
○─┴─╯    base             ○─╯─╯    base
```

Ok, that explains it; tmux does indeed break the "zero config" mechanism. Right now, all we can do is ask the terminal for its XTVERSION, and see if it is ghostty or kitty with a new enough version; but tmux doesn't forward that, but answers it itself.

We might invest in a better detection mechanism in the future, but it would require cooperation from terminal authors, so it will take a while to design and implement. (And it still wouldn't work for fonts that contain these symbols, e.g. if they are added to nerd fonts one day.)

I ran into the same limitation a few times, and decided to fix it slightly differently: I made the clipboard completely global, so that it even allows you to cherry-pick between unrelated repos. This can be useful when you have several independent checkouts of the same repo, or when you want to copy between different forks of the same base repo; the user is then responsible for fetching the required objects in the destination first. Of course, pasting into a completely unrelated repo gives a "Fatal: bad object" error, but I'd say that's fine; users are unlikely to expect this to work.

There's a reason why we don't highlight the whole line: with diff renderers that color the background green or red (e.g. delta), it's impossible to see which lines are added and which ones are deleted. Now, for a raw git diff this isn't as much of an issue, but I still find its red/green text hard to read on a blue background, so I decided to use the narrower highlight for all diffs. In an earlier draft I had it configurable per diff renderer (not all of them use the background color the way delta does), but then decided that the flexibility isn't needed.

Side note: if you are not using a [diff renderer](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit/blob/master/docs/Custom_DiffRenderers.md), you are missing out. I recommend delta myself.

The problem is two-fold. First (and this is probably more of a bug), the sidebar highlight overlaps line numbers when setting `line-numbers = true` in delta's config. This makes the sidebar highlight visually confusing even without considering whole line highlighting because it conflicts with delta's line-number color settings. The number of colored spaces is hardcoded 2 and can't be changed.

Second is that the replacement is fundamentally not the same as the previous full line highlight. If I could use an analogy, the current behavior is like using a finger to point to a line you're reading in a book vs highlighting the line. Spelling out the cycle/diamond handling, since it's cheaper than it looks — no new merge semantics are needed:

**Linearize, then reuse the existing rules.** Resolve `import:` entries depth-first in listed order into the same ordered file list `loadUserConfig` already consumes. The current rules then apply unchanged: per-key override with last-file-wins, `customCommands` appended across files, `Validate()` per file. A diamond (A imports B and C, both import D) resolves exactly like listing those files in `LG_CONFIG_FILE` today — same order-dependence, no new conflict-resolution logic.

**Cycles:** keep a visited set of canonicalized absolute paths (`filepath.Abs` + `EvalSymlinks`, so `./tags.yml`, `tags.yml`, and symlinked spellings compare equal) and merge each file once — `#pragma once` semantics. An optional depth cap is a cheap backstop, but the visited set alone terminates.

So the "already supported" part is real: ordering, override, and append semantics all exist and are documented; an `import:` key would only change how the file list is assembled, not how it's merged.

I personally don't use delta or any other other diff renderer–I actually prefer the default git diff view, it just makes more sense to my brain–and with the default git diff the two character highlight is hard to use. While I am all for increasing compatibility with other tools, I think it is important to recognize that while lazygit and delta work well together, at the end of the day lazygit is a git client, and should work well out-of-the-box with the default tools git gives, not require yet another tool for optimal performance. Having only 4 characters of highlight makes it hard for me to tell which line are actually being selected, especially in wide windows, which I usually use.

I am strongly in favor of bringing back the full-width highlight, either universally or per-tool. Since I only have the one tool, the default git diff, those are the same to me.

Some ways to do this I have thought of:
1. Have a single global setting -- doesn't play nice with different renderer styles, as noted above
2. Have per-tool overrides -- unnecessary complicated to configure for those of us who just use the default git diff
3. Combine 1 + 2: global default + per-tool overrides -- my preference; allows for easy configuration, while still letting power users have different settings for each tool
4. Combine 1 + 2, and set sensible defaults -- taking option 3 a step further, you can set sensible per-tool defaults (e.g. git diff uses full-width, delta uses two characters, etc.), while still letting users override that setting as they desire. Ideally the global default will still override these defaults, so users can trivially set a uniform behavior should they desire that.

I think option 4 will provide the best out-of-the-box experience, but will also understandably be the most work, but I personally will be happy with any of the 4.
